title: Bengaluru CA's Viral Post Challenges India's Wedding Spending Culture
excerpt: A former KPMG and Deloitte employee urged couples to stop spending Rs 20 lakh on weddings to impress relatives, arguing the food lasts two hours but the financial burden lasts years.
body:
• A Bengaluru-based chartered accountant and former KPMG and Deloitte employee sparked a viral debate by urging couples to stop spending Rs 20 lakh on weddings to impress relatives
  • The post argued that wedding food "lasts 2 hours" while the financial burden "lasts years," resonating with a growing pushback against India's wedding spending culture
  • India's wedding industry is valued at an estimated Rs 10 lakh crore, with average middle-class celebrations costing Rs 15-25 lakh in major cities
  • The viral discussion reflects a broader generational shift, with younger professionals increasingly questioning the social pressure behind extravagant celebrations

A Bengaluru-based chartered accountant who previously worked at KPMG and Deloitte has ignited a viral debate on social media after urging Indian couples to rethink the financial burden of lavish weddings, arguing that spending Rs 20 lakh to impress relatives leaves lasting damage on household finances.

The Viral Post

The professional, whose post was covered by NDTV, Moneycontrol, and The Economic Times, laid out a straightforward calculation that struck a nerve with millions of Indians navigating the social pressures of wedding spending. The central argument: the food at a wedding "lasts 2 hours" while "the bill lasts years."

The post questioned why couples and their families take on significant debt to fund a single evening of celebrations — catering, venue, decorations, and entertainment — primarily to maintain appearances before extended family and community members who contribute little to the couple's financial future.

Rather than spending Rs 20 lakh or more on a single event, the CA suggested redirecting those funds toward the couple's financial foundation: a home down payment, investments, emergency savings, or business capital. The post resonated particularly with salaried professionals in cities like Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi, where the gap between wedding expectations and household incomes has widened sharply.

"India's wedding industry is valued at an estimated Rs 10 lakh crore, according to the Confederation of All India Traders, with projections of continued growth."

India's Wedding Spending Problem

The viral post taps into a growing tension in Indian society. India's wedding industry is valued at an estimated Rs 10 lakh crore, according to the Confederation of All India Traders, with projections of continued growth. Average middle-class weddings in major cities now cost between Rs 15-25 lakh, with destination weddings and premium venues pushing costs well above Rs 50 lakh.

The spending is not limited to the affluent. Studies have documented that Indian families across income brackets routinely spend one to three years' worth of household income on weddings, with many taking on substantial debt. A significant portion of wedding expenses are driven by social obligations — feeding hundreds of guests, often including distant relatives and acquaintances the couple may rarely interact with again.

Catering alone accounts for 40-50 percent of total wedding costs, according to industry data. At premium venues in Bengaluru, per-plate costs range from Rs 1,300 to Rs 3,500, with guest lists routinely exceeding 500 people.

The Generational Shift

The post sparked thousands of comments and shares, revealing a clear generational divide. Younger professionals, particularly those in the tech and finance sectors, largely agreed with the sentiment, sharing their own frustrations with wedding expectations.

Critics argued that weddings hold cultural and emotional significance beyond their price tags, and that the comparison between food lasting two hours and bills lasting years oversimplifies a deeply personal family decision. Some pointed out that weddings also serve as rare occasions for extended families to gather, particularly for diaspora families whose members are scattered across cities and countries.

Others noted a growing trend of couples opting for intimate, budget-conscious celebrations — registered marriages followed by small dinners — though social pressure from parents and in-laws often makes this difficult in practice.

A Financial Perspective

From a financial planning standpoint, the CA's argument carries weight. A Rs 20 lakh investment made at age 25, compounding at 12 percent annually, would grow to approximately Rs 1.9 crore by age 55. Alternatively, the same amount could cover a substantial down payment on a home in many Indian cities, eliminating years of rent.

Financial advisors have increasingly encouraged couples to have open conversations about wedding budgets, setting expectations early with families and distinguishing between essentials and obligations driven purely by social comparison. The trend aligns with a broader movement toward financial literacy and transparency among India's urban middle class.

For the Indian diaspora, where weddings frequently span multiple countries and involve international travel for guests, the financial calculus is even more complex — making the debate about value versus show particularly relevant.
